parole.significato: Pompous, officious talk.
parole.testo: From Middle English blusteren (“to wander about aimlessly”); however, apparently picking up the modern sense from Middle Low German blüstren (“to blow violently”; compare later Low German blustern, blistern). parole.significato: A spar projecting over the prow of a sailing vessel to provide the means of adding sail surface.
parole.testo: First attested in late 13th century. Probably borrowed from Middle Low German bochspret, from boch (“bow of a ship”) + spret (“pole”) (related to Old English spreot and English sprout).

parole.significato: A type of machine for bending sheet metal. (See wikipedia.)
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Middle Low German brake, Dutch braak, Old Dutch braeke; possibly related to sense 1.

parole.significato: A hardened rectangular block of mud, clay etc., used for building.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English brik, bryke, bricke, from Middle Low German and Middle Dutch bricke ("cracked or broken brick; tile-stone"; modern Dutch brik), ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *brekan (“to break”), whence also Old French briche and French brique (“brick”). parole.significato: To bend; buckle.
parole.testo: From dialectal buck ("to give in, yield"; also bug (“to bend”)), from Middle Low German bucken (“to bend”) or Middle Dutch bucken, bocken (“to bend”), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *bukkōn (“to bend, bend repeatedly”), from Proto-Germanic *bukkōną (“to bend”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰugʰ-,

parole.significato: An Asian plant, of the species Fagopyrum esculentum.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Middle Low German bōkwête (“beech-wheat”) (so called because of its triangular seeds, which resemble the much larger seeds of the beech nut from the beech tree, and the fact that it is used like wheat), probably via Middle Dutch boecweit, boecweite. parole.significato: Lively, lusty.
parole.testo: From Middle English cant, kaunt, presumably from Middle Low German *kant, perhaps a slang word related to kant (“edge, rim”), from Medieval Latin canthus. Attested from the 13th or 14th century.

parole.significato: A narrow board, usually thicker at one edge than the other, used as siding for houses and similar structures of frame c…
parole.testo: From Middle English clapholt, partial translation from Middle Low German klappholt or Middle Dutch klapholt (“barrel stave”), from klappen (“to crack”) + holt (“wood”). The part "holt" was later calqued to "board".

parole.significato: To walk in a heavy, noisy manner.
parole.testo: Origin obscure. Likely from Middle Low German klunden (“to rumble, make noise, swallow loudly, gurgle, speak in a gurgling manner”). Compare also Scots clunk (“to walk heavily”), where the shift from -t to -k is a regular occurrence.

parole.significato: A large basket, especially as used for coal.
parole.testo: From Middle English corf, borrowed from Middle Low German korf or Middle Dutch korf, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *korb.

parole.significato: A contemptible or inferior dog.
parole.testo: From Middle English curre (“watchdog, small hunting dog, mongrel, mutt”), perhaps of Middle Low German or North Germanic origin, possibly from Old Norse kurr (“grumbling”), itself of imitative origin. Compare Middle Dutch corre (“domestic dog, yard dog, watch-dog”), dialectal Dutch korre (“dog, yard

parole.significato: Chiefly followed by away: to spend (time) without haste or purpose.
parole.testo: The verb is possibly: * a variant of daddle (“(Britain, dialectal) to walk or work slowly, dawdle, saunter, trifle”) or doddle (“(Britain, dialectal) to walk feebly or slowly, dawdle, idle, saunter, stroll”), possibly influenced by daw (“(Britain, dialectal) lazy, good-for-nothing person, sluggard”)

parole.significato: A division, a portion, a share, a part, a piece.
parole.testo: From Middle English del, dele, from Old English dǣl (“part, share, portion”), from Proto-West Germanic *daili, from Proto-Germanic *dailiz (“part, deal”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰ(h₁)-oy-lo- (“part, watershed”). Cognate with Scots dele (“part, portion”), West Frisian diel (“part, share”), Dutch

parole.significato: Wood that is easy to saw (from conifers such as pine or fir).
parole.testo: From Middle English dele (“plank”), from Middle Low German dele, from Old Saxon thili, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *þiljǭ (“plank, board”); cognate with Old English þille. Doublet of (dialectal) theal and thill.

parole.significato: A small Dutch coin, equivalent to one-eighth of a stiver.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German doyt, cognate with Middle Dutch duit. Doublet of thwaite.

parole.significato: To be weakly or foolishly fond of somebody.
parole.testo: The verb is derived from Middle English doten, from Middle Low German doten (“to be foolish”) or Middle Dutch doten (“to be silly”). Doublet of doit (Scottish English). The noun in the sense of "imbecile" is derived from Middle English dote (“simpleton”), itself from doten (see above). The noun in t

parole.significato: A person who is habitually drunk.
parole.testo: From earlier droncarde, from Middle English *druncard (attested as a surname, Druncard), possibly from Middle Low German drunkert, equivalent to drunk + -ard (“pejorative agent suffix”). Compare German Trunkart. Compare braggart.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Netherlands, the Dutch people or the Dutch language.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tewtéh₂ From Middle English Duch (“German, Low German, Dutch”), from Middle Low German dütsch, düdesch (“German, Low German, Dutch”) and Middle Dutch dūtsch, dūtsc (“German, Low German, Dutch”), from Proto-West Germanic *þiudisk, from Proto-Germanic *þiudiskaz (“of one’s people”), derived

parole.significato: Any of the triangular blades at the end of an anchor, designed to catch the ground.
parole.testo: Mid-16th century in the sense of “anchor blade”. Probably the same word as in etymology 2 above or else a related word for something flat (cf. Proto-Germanic *flakaz). parole.significato: Uncommon; out of the ordinary; extraordinary; superior.
parole.testo: From Middle English forby, forbi, of Middle Low German or North Germanic origin, equivalent to fore- + by. parole.significato: Despondent; moody; sullen.
parole.testo: Probably from Middle Low German glum (“glum”), related to German dialectal glumm (“gloomy, troubled, turbid”). More at gloomy.

parole.significato: To be frightened; also, to shudder with fear; to quake, to tremble.
parole.testo: From Middle English gruen, probably from Middle Low German gruwen or Middle Dutch gruwen (compare Dutch gruwen), both from Proto-Germanic *grūwijaną, perhaps ultimately an imitative derivative of Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰers- (“to bristle”), or instead from *gʰer- (“to rub, stroke, grind”).

parole.significato: A breach or hole made by the force of a torrent; fissure, chasm.
parole.testo: From Middle English gole (“a whirlpool, narrow inlet of the sea, ditch or stream”), from Middle Low German goel, gȫl, gȫle (“swamp, marshy lowland”), related to Old Dutch gulla (“pool, puddle”), Old French goille (“pool, puddle, pond”), all ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *goli, *golljā (“puddle

parole.significato: To propel oneself rapidly upward, downward and/or in any horizontal direction such that momentum causes the body to bec…
parole.testo: From Middle English jumpen (“to walk quickly, run, jump”), probably of Middle Low German or North Germanic origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *gumpōną ~ *gumbōną (“to hop, skip, bounce”), an iterative verb. The OED suggests an imitative origin. Related to jumble. In the sense “to propel oneself”

parole.significato: A readiness in performance; aptness at doing something.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, use as "special skill" from 1580. Possibly from 14th century Middle English krak, knack (“a sharp sound or blow”), knakke, knakken, from Middle Low German and of imitative origin, similar to Dutch knak (“snap, crack”). Latter cognate to German knacken (“to crack”). See also crac

parole.significato: A rounded protuberance, especially one arising from a flat surface; a fleshy lump or caruncle.
parole.testo: From Middle English knobbe, from Middle Low German knobbe (“knob, knot in wood, bud”), probably ultimately from a variant of Proto-Germanic *knappô (“knob, lump”), one of several kn- words related to *knudaną (“to knead”). parole.significato: A knob, usually ornamental
parole.testo: From Middle English knop, from Middle Low German and Middle Dutch knoppe, from Proto-Germanic *knuppô, *knuppaz, *knappô, which is perhaps related to *knappō (“knob, boy”). Possible doublet of knave and knob.

parole.significato: Relating to denominations belonging to a money of account formerly in extensive mercantile use in North Germany.
parole.testo: From Middle Low German lübsch or Middle Dutch lubesch, both ("of Lübeck"). Compare German lübisch (“of Lübeck”).

parole.significato: A light all-purpose cord commonly used to bind the end of a larger rope, to prevent fraying.
parole.testo: From Middle English merlin, from Middle Low German marling, from Middle Dutch marlijn (“cord”), from marlen (“secure, fasten”), frequentative of maren (“to moor”), from Proto-Germanic *mairōną (“to moor, fasten to”), from Proto-Indo-European *mer-.

parole.significato: A fellow, comrade, colleague, partner or someone with whom something is shared, e.g. shipmate, classmate.
parole.testo: From Middle English mate, a borrowing from Middle Low German mate (“messmate”) (replacing Middle English mett, mette (“table companion, mate, partner”), from Old English ġemetta (“sharer of food, table-guest”)), from Old Saxon gimato, derived from Proto-Germanic *gamatjô, itself from *ga- (“together

parole.significato: To rain in very fine drops.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English misellen (“to drizzle”), cognate with Low German miseln, musseln (“to mizzle”), Dutch miezelen (“to drizzle, rain gently”). parole.significato: Any of several trees, of the genus Morus, having edible fruits.
parole.testo: From Middle English mulbery, molberye, murberie, partly from Old English mōrberġe (“mulberry”) (q.v.), and probably partly from Middle Low German mulbere (“mulberry”), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *mūrubaʀi ~ *mōrubaʀi, from Latin mōrus + Proto-West Germanic *baʀi. parole.significato: To take a small, quick bite, or several of such bites, of (something).
parole.testo: The verb is derived from Late Middle English nebillen, nebyll (“to peck away at (something), nibble; (figurative) to attempt to sing (a part of a song)”); further etymology uncertain, possibly from Middle Low German nibbelen (“to eat in small bites, peck”) (modern German Low German nibbeln, gnibbeln

parole.significato: A small amount of food or drink, (particularly) a small amount of liquor.
parole.testo: Short for nipperkin, ultimately from Middle Low German nippen or Middle Dutch nipen ("to sip; nip"; > Dutch nippen). Compare also German nippen (“to sip; taste”).

parole.significato: The platform over the hold of a ship that makes up the fourth or lowest deck, hence in full called orlop deck, especial…
parole.testo: From Middle English overlop (“deck of a single-decker”), from Middle Low German overlop (“which leaps overhead”). Compare overloop.

parole.significato: To travel along (a road, path etc.).
parole.testo: Probably partly from Middle Low German pat, partly imitative. Some senses possibly influenced by pad (“soft part of an animal's foot”, noun).

parole.significato: To talk insincerely; to prevaricate or equivocate in speech or actions.
parole.testo: Probably from Middle English *palter (“rag, trifle, worthless thing”), from Middle Low German palter (“rag, cloth”). More at paltry.

parole.significato: Mean; paltry.
parole.testo: From *palter (“a rag, worthless thing”), from Middle Low German palter (“rag, cloth”). More at paltry.

parole.significato: Trashy, trivial, of little value.
parole.testo: From Middle Low German paltrig (“ragged, rubbishy, worthless”), from palter, palte (“cloth, rag, shred”), from Old Saxon *paltro, *palto (“cloth, rag”), from Proto-Germanic *paltrô, *paltô (“scrap, rag, patch”). Of uncertain ultimate origin, but perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *polto- (“cloth”), se

parole.significato: To pamper.
parole.testo: From Middle English pampen, from Middle Low German pampen (“to pamper oneself, live luxuriously”), from Old Saxon *pampōn, from Proto-West Germanic *pampōn, from Proto-Germanic *pampōną (“to swell”), from Proto-Indo-European *bamb- (“round object”). Cognate with West Frisian pampe (“to stuff, cram”)

parole.significato: A tattered or worthless piece of clothing; a rag.
parole.testo: Uncertain; possibly related to pelting (“mean, paltry”) (obsolete), peltry (“rubbish, trash; an unpleasant thing”) (chiefly Scotland, obsolete), and paltry (“of little value, trashy, trivial; contemptibly unimportant, despicable”), possibly from a Germanic language such as Middle Low German palte, p

parole.significato: A small, usually round or cylindrical object designed for easy swallowing, usually containing some sort of medication.
parole.testo: From Middle English pille (also pillem), a borrowing from Middle Low German pille or Middle Dutch pille (whence Dutch pil), probably from Latin pila, pilula. * (persuade or convince): Generalized from red pill.

parole.significato: To pamper.
parole.testo: From Middle English pompen. Possibly an alteration of pampen (English pamp), from Middle Low German pampen (“to pamper oneself, live luxuriously”), from Old Saxon *pampōn, from Proto-Germanic *pampōną (“to swell”), from Proto-Indo-European *bamb- (“round object”).

parole.significato: The small European lamprey species Petromyzon branchialis.
parole.testo: From Middle English pryde, from Middle Low German lampride, from Medieval Latin lampreda.

parole.significato: A thin, pointed, projecting part, as of an antler or a fork or similar tool.
parole.testo: From Middle English pronge, perhaps from Middle Low German prange (“stick, restraining device”), from prangen (“to press, pinch”), from Old Saxon *prangan, from Proto-West Germanic *prangan, from Proto-Germanic *pranganą (“to press”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)preng- (“to wrap up, constrict”). parole.significato: A cat.
parole.testo: Probably from Middle Low German pūse, pūskatte or Dutch poes (“puss, cat”, also slang for “vulva”), ultimately from a common Germanic word for cat, perhaps ultimately imitative of a sound made to get its attention (compare Arabic بسة (bissa)). parole.significato: A German count whose hereditary lands are in the Rheingau area north of the river Rhine, especially one descended from…
parole.testo: From Middle Low German ringrave and German Rheingraf, from Rhein (“the river Rhine”) + Graf (“grave, count”).

parole.significato: cat meat
parole.testo: From roof + rabbit. From the common habit of cats to prowl on rooftops, and the meat being sold or passed off as rabbit. Similar formations exist in several European languages. parole.significato: The state of sinking or bending; a droop.

parole.significato: A layer of impurities that accumulates at the surface of a liquid (especially molten metal or water).
parole.testo: From Middle English scum, scome, skum, skome, scumme, from Middle Low German or Middle Dutch schūme (“foam”), from Old Dutch *scūm, from Frankish *skūm, from Proto-Germanic *skūmaz (“froth, foam”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH- (“to cover, conceal”). Cognate with Dutch schuim (“foam”), West Fri

parole.significato: A seaman; mariner; skipper.
parole.testo: Either formed anew from ship + -er or borrowed from Middle Low German schipper; compare skipper and Old English sċipere (“sailor”). Piecewise doublet of skipper (“captain, sailor”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; perhaps; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: A weaned piglet; any piglet.
parole.testo: From Middle English schote, of uncertain origin. Perhaps a special use of Middle English schote (“projectile, young shoot”), or perhaps of Middle Low German origin, cognate with West Flemish schote (“young piglet”).

parole.significato: An arrangement of sheaves for drying; a stook.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English schok, from Old English *sċoc or Middle Low German schok; in any case, from Proto-West Germanic *skok and possibly related to Latvian kàudze and Lithuanian kiūgis.

parole.significato: The husk of oats after it has been threshed.
parole.testo: From Middle Low German schôde, from Old Saxon *skōda, from Proto-West Germanic *skaudā, from Proto-Germanic *skaudō (“sheath, husk”), from Proto-Indo-European *skewdʰ- (“to cover, surround, enwrap”). Cognate with Middle Dutch schode (“pod, shell, husk”), German Schote (“pod, hull”), Icelandic skauð

parole.significato: To writhe the body so as to produce friction against one's clothes, as do those who have the itch.
parole.testo: From Middle English shuggen, shoggen, schoggen (“to shake, shake off, mix by shaking, tremble, shake loose from one's clothing”), probably a variant of Middle English schokken (“to move rapidly, shake, push”), from Middle Low German schocken (“to shake, tremble”). See schokken.

parole.significato: To strain, as milk; pass through a strainer or anything similar; filter.
parole.testo: From Middle English silen, sylen, from Middle Low German silen ("to let off water, filter, strain"; > Low German silen, sielen), equivalent to sie (“to filter, strain”) + -le. parole.significato: A shin of beef.
parole.testo: Possibly from Middle Low German schink, schinke, schenke (“leg; shank; shin bone; ham”), from Old Saxon skinka, from Proto-West Germanic *skinkō (“shank; thigh; that which is bent”), from Proto-Germanic *skinkô, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)keng- (“to limp; to be crooked, slant”). The word is cognat

parole.significato: Waste material from a mine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German slagge, slaggen (“slag, dross”), from Old Saxon *slaggo, from Proto-West Germanic *slaggō, from Proto-Germanic *slaggô, from Proto-Germanic *slagōną (“to strike”) + *-gô (diminutive suffix). parole.significato: A broad, flat, wooden bar, a slat, especially as used to secure a door, window, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English slot, from Middle Low German slot or Middle Dutch slot, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *slot, from Proto-Germanic *slutą, related to the verb *sleutaną (“to lock”). parole.significato: A small sailing vessel, commonly rigged as a sloop, used chiefly in the coasting and fishing trade and often called a f…
parole.testo: From Middle Low German smack (Low German Schmacke, Schmaake (“small ship”)) or Dutch smak, perhaps ultimately related to smakken, imitative of the sails' noise.

parole.significato: A facial expression comprised by flexing the muscles of both ends of one's mouth, often showing the front teeth, withou…
parole.testo: From Middle English smilen (“to smile”), from Middle Low German *smîlen (“to smile”), from Middle High German smielen, from Old High German smielēn, from Proto-West Germanic *smīlēn, from Proto-Germanic *smīlāną (“to smile”), from Proto-Indo-European *smey- (“to laugh, be glad, wonder”). Cognate wit

parole.significato: To growl angrily by gnashing or baring the teeth; to gnarl; to utter grumbling sounds.
parole.testo: Frequentative of earlier snar (“to growl”), perhaps from Middle Low German snorren (“to drone”), of probably imitative origin. Equivalent to snar + -le. Related to German schnarren (“to rattle”) and schnurren (“to hum, buzz”).

parole.significato: The long, projecting nose, mouth, and jaw of a beast, as of pigs.
parole.testo: From Middle English snowte, snout, snute, from Old English *snūt, *snūte or Middle Low German snûte, from Proto-West Germanic *snūt, from Proto-Germanic *snūtaz. parole.significato: A cry with a short, sudden expulsion of breath.
parole.testo: From Middle English sobben, perhaps from Middle Low German sabben (“to drool, slobber, salivate”). parole.significato: A splinter, fragment or chip, especially of stone.
parole.testo: From Middle English spalle (“a chip”) (first documented in 1440), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from the Middle English verb spald (“to split”) (c.1400), from Middle Low German spalden, cognate with Old High German spaltan (“to split”).

parole.significato: Any of various microcrystalline minerals, of light, translucent, or transparent appearance, which are easily cleft.
parole.testo: From Middle Low German spar, sper (“spar”); or from a backformation of sparstone (“spar”), from Middle English sparston (“gypsum, chalk”), from Old English spærstān (“gypsum”). Related to German Sparkalk (“plaster”), Old English spæren (“of plaster, of mortar”).

parole.significato: To splash (someone or something) with small droplets.
parole.testo: Probably from Middle Low German or Dutch spatten (“to spout, burst”) + -er (frequentative suffix). Related to spit (“saliva”).

parole.significato: A narrow strip of wood split or peeled from a larger piece.
parole.testo: From Middle English splint, splent, splente, from Middle Low German splinte, splente or Middle Dutch splint, splinte. Cognate with Old High German splinza (“bar, bolt, latch”). parole.significato: A small shoot or twig of a tree or other plant; a spray.
parole.testo: From Middle English sprig, sprigge, of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Middle Low German sprik, spricke (“a dry, easily broken twig that has fallen from a tree; sprig”). parole.significato: Firm in standing or position; not tottering or shaking; fixed; firm.
parole.testo: From Middle English stedy, studi, stidiȝ, perhaps continuing Old English stæþþiġ, ġestæþþiġ (“steadfast, stable, firm, staid”), equivalent to stead + -y; or calquing Middle Low German or Middle Dutch stēdig. parole.significato: A pile or bundle, especially of straw.
parole.testo: From Middle English stowk, stouke, stouc, from or cognate with Middle Low German stûke (“bundle of grain”), from Middle Low German stûken (“to push, bump, compress”), from Old Saxon *stūkan, from Proto-Germanic *stūkaną (“to be stiff, push”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewg- (“to pound, push, beat

parole.significato: The remains of something that has been cut off; especially the remains of a tree, the remains of a limb.
parole.testo: From Middle English stumpe, stompe (“stump”), from or akin to Middle Low German stump (“stump”) or Middle Dutch stomp, from Old Saxon or Old Dutch *stump, from Proto-West Germanic *stump, from Proto-Germanic *stumpaz (“stump, blunt, part cut off”). parole.significato: A person from Sweden or of Swedish descent.

parole.significato: To engage in trade.

parole.significato: To move (something) with short, quick motions; to wobble.
parole.testo: From Middle English wagelen (attested in wagelyng), possibly a borrowing of Middle Low German wagelen; equivalent to wag + -le (“(frequentative)”). parole.significato: An area of wooden (especially oaken) panelling on the lower part of a room’s walls.
parole.testo: From Middle English waynscot, from Middle Low German wagenschot or Middle Dutch waghenscote, assumed to be from wagen (“wagon”) (from Old Saxon wagan) + schot, meaning “partition, crossbar," which is from or related to skiotan (“to shoot”).

parole.significato: The path left behind a ship on the surface of the water.
parole.testo: Probably from Middle Low German or Middle Dutch wake, from or akin to Old Norse vǫk (“a hole in the ice”) ( > Danish våge, Icelandic vök), from Proto-Germanic *wakwō (“wetness”), from Proto-Indo-European *wegʷ- (“moist, wet”).

parole.significato: Anticlockwise, counter-clockwise.
parole.testo: First use appears c. 1513, from Middle Low German weddersins (also wēder-, -sinnes), from wed(d)der- (“wither-, against, opposite”) + genitive of sin (“direction, way”).
